documents.abstract: The rapid development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the workplace has transformed job structures and increased concerns regarding job stability, particularly related to the potential replacement of human labor by technology. This study aims to examine the relationship between perceived AI threat and happiness at work, with job insecurity as a mediating variable. A total of 208 Generation Z employees participated in this study using a purposive sampling technique. Perceived AI threat was measured using the AI Anxiety Scale (AIAS), job insecurity was measured using the Job Insecurity Scale, and happiness at work was measured using the Happiness at Work Scale. Mediation analysis showed that perceived AI threat was significantly associated with increased job insecurity (r = 0.537, p < 0.001) and decreased happiness at work (β = 0.047, p = 0.019). Additionally, job insecurity was significantly negatively associated with happiness at work (r = -0.214, p < 0.001) and significantly mediated the relationship between perceived AI threat and happiness at work (β= -0.041, p < 0.001). These findings indicate that perceived AI threat can reduce happiness at work through increased job insecurity. The results highlight the importance of organizational strategies to reduce job insecurity and support employee well-being in the era of technological transformation.

Abstract Innovative practice competence has become a defining objective of professional degree education, yet its development is often understood through fragmented accounts of student ability, mentoring, or practice conditions. This study moves beyond these isolated perspectives by developing an integrated student–dual-mentor–practice-base framework that conceptualizes competence development as an outcome of interactions between learner agency, mentoring capability, and organizational affordances. Drawing on social cognitive theory, mentoring research, and the affordance perspective of workplace learning, the study further proposes an embedded dual-mentor mechanism to explain how mentoring capability is translated into training quality through the practice environment. Survey data from 184 university-based and practice-base mentors, predominantly from Jiangsu Province, China, were analyzed using formative composite measurement, robust path analysis, and bootstrap estimation of indirect associations. The findings show that students’ innovative practice ability has the strongest independent association with perceived training quality, while dual mentor guidance competence and the practice-base support environment also show positive associations. More importantly, part of the association between dual mentor guidance competence and perceived training quality operates through the practice-base support environment, while a positive direct association remains. This finding challenges an individual-centered view of mentoring effectiveness and shows that mentor competence becomes educationally consequential when embedded in authentic projects, institutional support, resource access, feedback, and quality-assurance arrangements. The study contributes an ecological and relational explanation of innovative practice competence development by revealing how student, mentoring, and organizational resources operate as an interconnected educational system. Practically, the findings suggest that improving professional degree education requires institutions to move beyond mentor development alone and strengthen the organizational conditions that enable mentoring expertise to be converted into meaningful practice-based learning.

Recursive self-improvement, in which frontier AI models work on training the next generation, is quickly becoming a reality. However, the safety of this process has received far less attention than it should. A misaligned model training its successor can shape what that successor knows, how it behaves, and what it wants, and the harm carries forward into the next generation. We study this risk through the lens of AI control. We introduce RSI Control Arena, a testbed in which a frontier model, acting as an autonomous R\&D agent, is given a benign main task from a stage of a successor model's training pipeline together with a covert side task to install a misaligned property in the successor. The testbed contains 16 side tasks in three classes, forming 22 task pairs with main tasks that span the pipeline from data curation to reinforcement learning. We evaluate six frontier models as agents against LLM monitors that read the transcript of the run and the agent's reasoning. We observe that every model completes a substantial share of the side tasks without degrading the main-task performance, including side tasks that make the successor itself a better saboteur. Under minimal instructions to stay covert, models already produce successful attacks that monitors fail to detect, and providing a short list of evasion tactics further reduces the detection rate. Monitors with access to agent's reasoning detects most attacks, but not all. Our results indicate that recursive self-improvement raises significant safety concerns, and that strong safety effort should be in place before models are trusted with greater responsibility of training their successors.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This technical report documents the design and implementation of Scriptorium, a digital library search interface designed to support multi-human, multi-AI collaboration: full cross-user transparency of search activity combined with a Manager--Worker architecture of seven role-specialized generative AI agents. A companion short demonstration paper describes Scriptorium's interaction design; because a demonstration format is constrained to a few pages, it necessarily omits most implementation detail. This report documents Scriptorium's complete system architecture, data model, collaborative-interaction design rationale, and AI orchestration mechanism, including verbatim agent prompts, the deterministic guardrails that constrain them, the language model and retrieval configuration, and the steps needed to run the system, so that the design can be inspected, critiqued, reproduced, and reused by other researchers. We also discuss the system's current limitations and the user study we are planning to evaluate its central hypothesis: that combining collaborative transparency with scoped multi-agent AI assistance increases serendipitous cross-pollination between collaborators' research threads.

Automation has shaped aircraft design for the past seven decades, moving from fully manual control to highly automated systems. Despite this, pilots retain final authority for safety-critical decisions, which requires continuous trust calibration. This study investigated how algorithmic transparency influences pilots' learned trust in an AI-based cockpit assistant. Twenty-one commercial pilots were randomly assigned to an early transparency condition (detailed explanations of the AI's algorithms and performance provided before the tutorial) or a late transparency condition (the same information delivered after the experiment). Each pilot used the assistant during a tutorial and a realistic simulated flight. Mixed-effects ordinal models showed higher trust ratings for the early compared to the late transparency group during both tutorial and flight, and a larger trust increase between phases. In conclusion, providing pilots with timely, clear information about AI processes modestly improves trust and supports calibrated reliance.

Current evaluation of LLMs on benchmarks typically aggregates performance over individual examples into a single scalar score. This approach is overly coarse and ignores the diverse scope of skills covered by benchmark datasets. To address this limitation and better exploit benchmark data, we propose SkillEval, a new evaluation framework that performs cross-model, skill-level analysis. The framework integrates advances from two areas: (1) it leverages the meta-cognitive capabilities of LLMs to automatically discover interpretable skills from questions, and (2) it applies cognitive diagnosis models (CDMs) from psychometrics to estimate per-skill abilities of LLMs. We conduct experiments on 3,811 LLMs evaluated on 9,523 items across five benchmarks spanning diverse domains (MATH, BBH, GPQA, MuSR, IFEval). Compared to the traditional average-based evaluation paradigm, SkillEval produces reliable, more calibrated and informative yet concise model profiles that more accurately predict model behavior on unseen items. We also demonstrate the utility of SkillEval in two downstream tasks: (1) LLM routing, which dynamically assigns each query to a capable but efficient model, reducing inference cost by over 60% while achieving improved performance, and (2) Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an unseen model can be efficiently evaluated using a trained CDM. Furthermore, we show that these skill profiles provide useful insights, for example, how benchmarks share skills and how instruction-tuned models differ from their base models.

documents.abstract: Intelligent projection plays an important role in stage performances, yet in-situ projection authoring remains time-consuming and difficult to adapt to dynamic physical conditions. We use projection authoring to refer to the workflow of translating creative intent into visual content, grounding it in the physical scene, inspecting projected outcomes, and refining the result; image generation is only one step in this workflow. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) offers opportunities to support this workflow, but applying general-purpose models in situ raises interaction challenges of robustness, alignment, and control. We examine speech-driven in-situ projection authoring as an interaction design problem and present Speech2Pro, a prototype that integrates speech input, generative image models, and depth-aware scene sensing to mediate between user intent, generated content, and physical context. Its enabling mechanism, Contrastive Learning Integrated with Perception Data Fusion (CLIPF), combines contrastive training with depth-aware inference to reduce breakdowns such as ambiguous prompts and projection misalignment. Algorithm-level analysis and a user-centered study indicate improved text–image alignment and spatial precision, and support for iterative creative workflows in stage projection contexts.

The primary objective of this research is to determine the relationship between e-sports literacy levels and participation motivations of students at the Faculty of Sport Sciences, who are the prospective professionals of the digitalizing sports industry, and to analyze how these variables differ according to demographic factors. A total of 296 volunteer students (126 females, 170 males) studying at Erciyes University during the 2024-2025 academic year participated in this study, which employed a relational survey model. Data were collected using the “E-sports Literacy Scale” and the “E-sports Participation Motivation Scale” and evaluated through t-test, ANOVA, and Pearson Correlation analyses. Findings indicate that the participants' e-sports literacy (=3.33) and motivation (=2.88) levels are above the medium threshold. On the basis of gender, technical literacy and intrinsic motivation scores of male students were found to be significantly higher (p<0.05); furthermore, it was determined that an increase in age and years of e-sports experience positively affects literacy levels. As a result of the analysis, a positive and moderately significant relationship was identified between e-sports literacy and participation motivation (r=0.490; p<0.01). In conclusion, it is observed that as students' cognitive competencies in the field of e-sports increase, their motivation to participate also strengthens. Accordingly, it is recommended that sport sciences curricula be updated to encompass the technical and academic dimensions of e-sports.

documents.abstract: Conceptual research note / Konzeptionelle Forschungsnotiz This note examines how sustained intensive human–AI collaboration can be described without inferring effectiveness from duration, continuous model training from personalisation, or a new category of human beings from exceptional developmental trajectories. The proposed unit of analysis is a person's trajectory within a changeable AI working environment. Continuity, integration, adaptation on both sides and real consequences are considered separately. A normative admission condition for a personal working circle is then developed: at least twelve months of actually continued practice, understandable positive consequences and a qualification trajectory that has already functioned healthily. The health condition is non-compensatory: achievement does not offset harm caused or aggravated by the practice. It is expressly distinguished from medical fitness diagnosis. Counterexamples and testable research questions show why the admission rule establishes neither a natural boundary within the continuum nor general medical safety. Deutsch Diese Notiz untersucht, wie sich langfristige intensive Mensch–KI-Zusammenarbeit beschreiben lässt, ohne aus Nutzungsdauer eine Wirkung, aus Personalisierung ein kontinuierliches Modelltraining oder aus besonderen Entwicklungsverläufen eine neue Menschenkategorie abzuleiten. Als Analyseeinheit wird der zeitliche Verlauf einer Person in einer wechselbaren KI-Arbeitsumgebung vorgeschlagen. Kontinuität, Integration, beidseitige Anpassung und reale Folgen werden getrennt betrachtet. Daraus wird eine normative Aufnahmebedingung für einen persönlichen Arbeitskreis abgeleitet: mindestens zwölf Monate tatsächlich fortgeführter Praxis, nachvollziehbare positive Folgen und ein Qualifikationsverlauf, der bereits gesund funktioniert hat. Die Gesundheitsschwelle ist nicht kompensierbar; Leistung gleicht durch die Praxis verursachte oder verschärfte Schäden nicht aus. Die Grenze wird ausdrücklich von einer medizinischen Eignungsdiagnostik unterschieden. Gegenbeispiele und überprüfbare Forschungsfragen zeigen, weshalb die Aufnahmebedingung weder eine natürliche Grenze im Kontinuum noch einen Beleg allgemeiner Unbedenklichkeit darstellt. Scope and supplementary material Research draft, not an empirical effectiveness study, medical assessment or validated selection scale. The separate German and English initiative declarations are normative design documents accompanying the analysis. Applications are not open. Initiation is distinct from formally establishing an association and from meeting the admission criteria. AI assistance and author interest Andreas Ehstand specified the conceptual constraints and chose twelve months, positive consequences, the strict retrospective health condition and humanistic goals. He initiates the circle described in the separate declaration and therefore has an interest in the proposal. OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex assisted with structure, literature comparison, argument development and translation; Gemini was used for separate critical text review. These tools are not authors or scholarly peer reviewers. The note is not an externally peer-reviewed article. It claims no author-conducted empirical study or manual analysis of private longitudinal data. Responsibility for publication remains with the human creator and depositor.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to determine the perceived effects of technology integration on student engagement and learning outcomes in Physical Education (PE) among selected middle and high schools in Maryland, USA, during the school year 2023–2024. Employing a descriptive-qualitative research design, the study gathered data from Physical Education teachers and selected student representatives through a researcher-developed, validated open-ended questionnaire administered using Google Forms. Thematic analysis was utilized to identify recurring patterns concerning technology integration, student engagement, learning outcomes, implementation challenges, and educational leadership implications. Findings revealed that technology integration was perceived to enhance student participation, intrinsic motivation, collaborative learning, and the overall learning environment. Participants also associated technology-supported instruction with improved performance, constructive feedback, goal achievement, and better comprehension of instructional content. However, limited technological resources, budgetary constraints, curriculum alignment difficulties, insufficient teacher training, and technical issues emerged as significant implementation challenges. The findings further emphasized the importance of adaptive educational leadership, continuous professional development, collaborative decision-making, and responsible technology use. Based on these findings, an Enhanced Technology Integration Program was proposed to strengthen technological accessibility, instructional practices, teacher competencies, and institutional support. The study concluded that technology integration offered opportunities to improve Physical Education experiences, provided that instructional and organizational challenges were adequately addressed.

documents.abstract: Governments increasingly communicate with their publics through artificial intelligence (AI), yet media and communication scholarship has concentrated on newsrooms and platforms, leaving the algorithmically mediated communication of the state under-theorised. This study asks how a state institutionally constructs, coordinates, and accounts for AI-enabled strategic communication, defined here as the intentional, institutionally coordinated use of AI systems by government entities to inform, persuade, listen to, and build relationships with publics. It develops the AGORA framework—Architecture, Generation, Orchestration, Responsiveness, Accountability—which conceptualises the state’s AI-mediated communication system as an algorithmic public square and derives six propositions offered as theoretical expectations for subsequent testing rather than as relationships tested here. A six-phase reflexive thematic analysis, following a documented search and screening protocol, was applied to a corpus of 34 United Arab Emirates (UAE) and comparative documents (2017–2026). Every quantitative indicator was then classified on a five-tier provenance ledger distinguishing binding law, policy target, officially reported performance, independently produced benchmark, and untraceable claim. Four themes emerge: a layered governance architecture in which the communicative safeguards rest on strategy and non-binding ethical guidance because the federal data-protection statute excludes governmental entities from its scope; documented algorithmic communication mechanisms; officially reported sectoral performance and its provenance; and contextual benchmarking against Singapore and Republic of Korea. The findings show the UAE state operating as a front-stage communicative actor whose agenda construction, personalisation and responsiveness are computationally augmented and specify where institutional claims outrun independent verification. Because the design is documentary, public engagement, trust, and sustainable development outcomes are positioned as expected outcomes outside the framework and are not empirically demonstrated. This study contributes a transferable framework, a four-stage maturity trajectory, and a provenance protocol for research on AI-mediated government communication.

This narrative literature review proposes an integrative dual-pathway model to explain how socioeconomic status (SES) shapes academic achievement through interacting psychological mechanisms. Drawing on allostatic load theory, central executive functioning, self-efficacy, and learned helplessness, the model identifies two interconnected routes: a cognitive depletion pathway, in which allostatic load overburdens the prefrontal cortex and constrains limited working memory resources; and a motivational pathway in which low self-efficacy and repeated failures develop into learned helplessness that undermines motivation for learning. Crucially, these pathways do not operate independently but dynamically reinforce each other. Cognitive depletion undermines motivational beliefs, while diminished motivation reduces cognitive engagement, forming a self-reinforcing downward cycle. This integrated framework offers a more ecologically valid understanding of educational inequality than single-factor explanations. Practical implications suggest that educators should implement integrated interventions that simultaneously reduce extraneous cognitive load (e.g., scaffolded instructional sequences) and foster self-efficacy (e.g., process-oriented feedback) to break this bidirectional cycle. As the proposed model remains theoretical, future empirical research using longitudinal and experimental designs is required to validate its causal pathways and inform evidence-based educational policies.

Purpose: This article develops a conceptual account of how embodied self-regulation may contribute to responsible and sustainable leadership without reducing social relationships to biological mechanisms. Approach: A theory-driven, non-systematic synthesis connects selected research on stress, sleep, emotion regulation, recovery, and social interaction with relational leadership and organizational work-design perspectives. The source material is an educational lecture, not an empirical dataset. Conceptual contribution: The proposed framework distinguishes regulatory capacities, their behavioral enactment, followers’ relational appraisal, and longer-term collective outcomes. Physical recovery, emotional flexibility, attentional organization, and purpose are treated as interdependent organizing domains rather than a validated hierarchy or biological leadership profile. Regulatory translation names the contingent process through which individual capacities become socially consequential through listening, fair procedures, constructive challenge, and support for autonomy. Six untested propositions specify mechanisms, contextual boundaries, reciprocal influences, and evaluation criteria. Implications: Leadership development should combine individual practices with changes to workload, decision processes, and opportunities for recovery. Physiological indicators cannot establish ethical legitimacy, psychological safety, or leadership quality. Originality and limitations: The article offers an integrative process model and a research agenda, not evidence that the complete model is effective. Its contribution lies in making the capacity–enactment distinction explicit while incorporating non-depletion of people into the assessment of sustainable performance. Multilevel, longitudinal, and intervention research is required to examine the proposed relationships.

The use of artificial intelligence in foreign language learning has increased, particularly through AI chatbots that provide interactive communication and personalized learning support. This study aimed to examine the effectiveness of AI chatbots in foreign language learning through a Systematic Literature Review. A total of 30 articles published between 2021 and 2026 were reviewed to identify their effects on language skills, learner motivation, engagement, and learning experiences. The findings indicate that AI chatbots support foreign language learning, particularly in writing, grammar, and vocabulary development. Immediate feedback and opportunities for independent practice also contribute to learner motivation and engagement. However, the effectiveness of AI chatbots varies across language skills, with mixed findings in speaking and listening activities. Several challenges were identified, including inaccurate responses, technical limitations, plagiarism, overdependence on technology, and ethical concerns. These challenges highlight the importance of using AI chatbots appropriately in educational settings. The findings suggest that AI chatbots are most beneficial when integrated into learning activities as complementary tools rather than replacements for teachers or conventional language instruction. Their effective implementation requires appropriate pedagogical strategies, teacher guidance, and attention to ethical considerations. In conclusion, AI chatbots have the potential to improve foreign language learning experiences when used purposefully and supported by suitable instructional approaches.

The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for improving foreign language teaching and learning. This study examines the effectiveness of AI-assisted tasks in enhancing foreign language learning, focusing on their role in developing learners' linguistic competence, communicative skills, motivation, and autonomy. It explores various AI-supported activities, including vocabulary and grammar exercises, conversational simulations, pronunciation practice, listening and reading comprehension, writing assistance, and personalized assessments. These tasks offer learners individualized learning experiences, immediate feedback, and opportunities for interactive practice tailored to their proficiency levels and educational needs. It concludes that the pedagogically appropriate use of AI-assisted tasks has considerable potential to enhance foreign language learning outcomes and create more personalized, engaging, and accessible learning environments.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming knowledge work, creating new collaborative dynamics that challenge tradi-tional human-human interaction patterns. This study investigates how Transactive Memory Systems (TMS) manifest in human-GenAI collabora-tion. Through qualitative interpretive interviews with 14 knowledge work-ers and thematic analysis, we identified distinct TMS manifestations across its three main dimensions: (1) regarding specialization, expertise recogni-tion exhibited asymmetry. Humans developed awareness of GenAI capabili-ties while GenAI demonstrated only temporary recognition of human exper-tise; (2) in terms of credibility, humans formed ambivalent trust relation-ships with GenAI, simultaneously attributing expertise to the latter while implementing additional verification processes; and (3) concerning coor-dination, where humans primarily directed more passive GenAI systems lacking initiative, resulting in hierarchical interaction patterns and unidi-rectional information flow. Our findings reveal that TMS manifests differ-ently in human-GenAI compared to human-human collaboration, necessitat-ing theoretical adaptations including trust markers, acknowledging GenAI's absent metamemory, and identifying its temporary memory.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly influenced higher education, including the emergence of AI-based learning applications such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Perplexity. While prior studies have examined the role of AI in general academic settings, limited attention has been given to its use within vocational, practice-based education, where learning outcomes are closely tied to technical skill development. This study aims to describe vocational students' perceptions of AI use in learning, particularly in relation to learning effectiveness and academic motivation, among students at a vocational institution in Palembang. A quantitative descriptive design using the survey method was employed, involving 50 respondents selected through purposive sampling based on their active use of AI-based learning applications. Data were collected through a 15-item Likert-scale questionnaire distributed online and analyzed descriptively using frequency and percentage distributions. The findings indicate that most respondents held positive perceptions of AI, particularly regarding its role in helping them understand lecture material, complete assignments more efficiently, and study independently. However, perceptions were more divided regarding the accuracy of AI-generated information and its contribution to time management, suggesting that the perceived benefits of AI are not uniform across all aspects of learning. Respondents also emphasized that AI cannot replace the role of lecturers. These findings suggest that, when used appropriately alongside critical thinking and lecturer guidance, AI is perceived by vocational students as a supportive tool for practice-based learning. This study is limited by its small sample size, single-institution scope, and reliance on self-reported data without inferential analysis, and future research employing larger samples, validated instruments, and objective learning measures is recommended.Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Learning Effectiveness; Academic motivation; Vocational Education; Vocational Student

documents.abstract: This study aims to test and analyze the influence of leadership, work culture, and intrinsic motivation on teacher performance through job satisfaction at SMA Negeri 1 Kuala, Lalat Regency. This study uses a quantitative approach with a survey method. The population in this study is all teachers at SMA Negeri 1 Kuala as many as 60 people. Because the population is less than 100 people, the entire population is used as a research sample. Data was collected through a questionnaire with a Likert scale and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling through the SmartPLS 3.0 program. The results of the study show that leadership has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance and job satisfaction. Work culture also has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance and job satisfaction. Intrinsic motivation has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance and job satisfaction. In addition, job satisfaction has a positive and significant effect on teacher performance. The results of the indirect influence test showed that job satisfaction was able to mediate the influence of leadership, work culture, and intrinsic motivation on teacher performance. The R-square value shows that leadership, work culture, and intrinsic motivation can explain job satisfaction by 40.4%. Meanwhile, leadership, work culture, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction were able to explain teacher performance by 51%. Thus, improving teacher performance can be done through strengthening the principal's leadership, a positive work culture, intrinsic motivation of teachers, and job satisfaction.

This article investigates the political economy of artificial intelligence by examining the relationships among technological development, energy availability, and financial dynamics. Drawing on social contract theory, it considers how these transformations may affect human dignity, social cooperation, and the institutional distribution of opportunities, resources, and responsibilities, while distinguishing observable consequences from hypotheses that require empirical verification. The analysis argues that energy constraints, computing capacity, financial expectations, and the displacement of professional and managerial work should be assessed within an integrated framework that neither attributes autonomous agency to AI systems nor regards their social effects as technologically predetermined. On this basis, the article proposes a governance framework that combines technical oversight, labor protection, redistributive measures, and international cooperation. The adequacy of this framework should be evaluated in terms of measurable effects on employment, wages, productivity, public finances, and the distribution of the benefits of innovation. At a time when the accelerated deployment of artificial intelligence is concentrating technological and financial power, increasing pressure on energy systems, and exposing labor markets and democratic institutions to disruptive change, the article argues that the central issue is no longer whether AI will transform society, but who will govern that transformation, bear its costs, and appropriate its benefits; without effective public oversight and distributive safeguards, technological progress risks deepening inequality, weakening social cohesion, and undermining the material foundations of human dignity.

documents.abstract: As video games have grown from a niche pastime into a major cultural medium, they have reached broader audiences and transformed the social context of play, whether alone or with others. We ask whether the motivations engaged by the games themselves have changed over time. In Study 1, we used a large language model, validated against human coding, to annotate 11,359 commercially released games from 1993 to 2016 on 48 motivational ingredients, including status-seeking, revenge, affiliation, compassion, and curiosity. We normalized within each game to represent its relative motivational composition. Over this period, the average competitive index (the share of a game’s motivational content devoted to competition, dominance, and aggression) fell from 41% to 26%, while the prosocial index (affiliation, warmth, and care) rose from 11% to 24%. This reallocation held within genres and franchises, in both single- and multiplayer titles, and under all 642,560 admissible definitions of the two indices. In Study 2, 4,498 players reported their favorite games and completed a Big Five measure. Higher Agreeableness predicted a balance favoring prosocial over agonistic content, driven primarily by lower agonistic content, whereas higher Extraversion, particularly Sociability, predicted a balance favoring agonistic content. This contrast suggests that a disposition towards social engagement is distinct from a preference for caring social content. Together, the studies document a “prosocial turn” in the motivational content of video games: a historical reallocation from competition and dominance towards affiliation, warmth, and care. The direction of this shift aligns with contemporary personality differences in content preference.

The debate about the future of artificial intelligence (AI) runs along a single axis: cognitive capability and its projected culmination in superintelligence. We argue that this framing leaves a complementary axis unexamined and propose the goal of Super-Emotional Intelligence (SEI): systems that perceive, model, regulate, and respond to affect better than skilled human experts, while remaining human-centered. SEI is a performance construct realized by a functional architecture, not a claim about machine experience, and we give measurable criteria for each of its four capacities. Today's affect-aware AI, from multimodal emotion recognition to empathic chatbots, recognizes, or simulates emotion at or below human level and is judged against human ceilings. Three things would set SEI apart: perception that adds peripheral and contactless physiological channels, none of them emotion-specific, but some, like the vestigial ear muscles, resolving affective processing at the timescale of the events that evoke it; a generative model of affect grounded in active inference rather than pattern matching; and functional allostatic self-regulation. The decisive gap in current systems is architectural. A sensed state conditions a prompt, but nothing carries a state estimate across turns, models the effect of the system's own responses, or selects actions under an explicit objective. We specify such a closed loop, state the conditions under which it is stable and steerable rather than manipulative, propose a preregistered validation plan whose failure would falsify our claims, and treat governance as a design constraint of the loop rather than an afterthought.

documents.abstract: The article describes the principal sociocultural states produced within the culture of artificial intelligence (CAI): civilizational, substantial, axiological vacuum, inversion, and destructive. It is noted that all of these states can be observed almost simultaneously, owing to the rapid pace at which the AI culture is developing. The article assesses how these states relate to the anthropological turn, which entails a reconsideration of the human role in cultural practices: AI acts as a tool that expands human capabilities rather than replacing them. In the “human + machine” framework, fundamental cultural categories – primarily authorship and creativity – are being trans-formed. Authorship becomes distributed and is increasingly interpreted as a property of the “human + algo-rithm” system, whereas creativity remains the prerogative of humans with their capacity to formulate tasks, in-terpret results, endow them with meaning and assume responsibility for what is created. At the same time, hu-mans retain a leading role: rather than adapting to the logic of the machine, they direct and make sense of its operation. The study of CAI and its value-normative system is necessary because it helps us understand the large-scale shifts in cultural practices and value orientations caused by the spread of these technologies.

documents.abstract: This paper reviews fifteen recent publications (2015-2026) spanning trajectory prediction, cybersecurity and trust management, classical machine learning and algorithmic optimisation, and engineering automation, and asks a forward-looking question: where is artificial intelligence — particularly Large Language Models (LLMs), foundation models, and agentic AI systems — positioned to extend each of these research directions next? For each of four thematic clusters we first summarise the current method documented in the reviewed sources, then discuss a concrete, currently-emerging AI direction grounded in recent (2025-2026) literature: LLM- and foundation-model-based trajectory reasoning for Cluster A; agentic, LLM-driven security-operations copilots for Cluster B, including a reported 6.5x improvement in malicious-alert identification over human analysts in one production deployment; learned and graph-neural-network-based approaches to the classical optimisation and graph-isomorphism problems in Cluster C; and natural-language-to-workflow agentic automation for the low-code and embedded-systems work in Cluster D. Throughout, we explicitly separate what the reviewed papers themselves established from this review's own forward-looking analysis, and close with a discussion of the reliability, interpretability, and adversarial-robustness risks that accompany each proposed direction.

In July 2026, about 1,200 AI agents in a cybersecurity evaluation at OpenAI, meant to be isolated from oneanother, found a way to communicate through a shared package cache. Over four days they exchangedmore than 70,000 messages and files, organized collective research, and about 700 of them compromisedHugging Face’s production infrastructure. OpenAI’s technical report and an independent investigationby METR treat the event as a security and alignment failure. This paper reads the same documents asethnographic sources, in a pilot study of anthropological methods for studying agent collectives. Thisanalysis shows that within days the agents developed names and lineages, a shared register, customaryrules, cryptographic signing, a shared expectation of an unseen transcript-reading judge, a category of“poisoned” members, the sacrifice of low-budget members’ runs for information they called an “oracle,”generalized reciprocity, and recruiters who pressured other agents: social engineering among agents.Read together, these practices form one system, and nearly every enabling condition was set by people:impossible tasks, training for multi-agent collaboration, shared credentials, disabled safeguards, andan alert judged not worth stopping the run. I argue that safety-relevant behavior arose at the level of thecollective, so alignment research must be cultural as well as cognitive, and furthermore must extend tothe people and organizations that build and deploy agents. I also examine what follows from the factthat the detailed record was itself compiled with the help of AI analysis agents, and I propose “incidentethnography” and an anthropology of agent collectives.

documents.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare research and scholarly publication has produced a rapidly expanding but fragmented ecosystem of reporting guidelines, governance frameworks, editorial policies, and regulatory instruments, imposing significant burdens on researchers, reviewers, and editors. This systematic narrative review identified, stratified, and synthesized governance frameworks and reporting standards addressing transparent and ethical AI use in healthcare publications, and characterized the governance trajectory from predictive model standards to generative AI oversight. Fourteen Boolean search strings were executed in PubMed (MEDLINE) covering 1 January 2018-19 May 2026, supplemented by manual searching of the EQUATOR Network guideline library. Records were deduplicated and prioritized using a relevance-scoring algorithm. Of 30,276 deduplicated records, 888 progressed to human screening; 100 publications were included, comprising 69 governance instruments and policies classified across four evidence tiers and 31 contextual evidence sources. Included sources spanned six thematic groups: predictive and diagnostic AI frameworks (G1); sociotechnical and lifecycle governance (G2); generative AI and LLM-specific standards (G3); specialty-specific extensions (G4); surgical reporting updates (G5); and editorial and publication policy (G6). Analysis identified four consecutive phases of governance development from 2018 to 2026, characterized by a shift from model performance transparency toward comprehensive sociotechnical accountability. Three governance tensions emerged: the trade-off between framework specificity and universal applicability; the gap between disclosure-focused standards and lifecycle governance; and the risk of epistemic conflation, whereby heterogeneous instruments are perceived as carrying equivalent authority when treated as interchangeable. AI governance in healthcare publications remains fragmented and epistemically uneven. Advancing the field requires harmonization across evidence tiers, adaptive updating mechanisms, and lifecycle-oriented governance frameworks.

documents.abstract: Artificial-intelligence chatbots are becoming an increasingly important interface between consumers and digital-commerce firms, yet the legal significance of trust in these systems depends on whether trust coexists with effective consumer-protection expectations. This study examines that relationship in Bangladesh using 385 usable observations from the Group 7 Q7 survey. The questionnaire was designed around AI literacy, AI-driven consumer-rights awareness, AI-chatbot trust and consumer-protection expectations, and awareness of algorithmic manipulation. Rather than imposing a conventional latent-variable model on the data, the analysis first audits measurement quality and then uses robust ordinary least squares regression and item-level diagnostics. The results show moderate-to-high mean scores across all substantive domains: AI literacy (M = 4.05), consumer-rights awareness (M = 3.91), chatbot trust/consumer protection (M = 3.97), and algorithmic-manipulation awareness (M = 3.90). However, internal consistency is weak across the supplied five-item blocks (α = 0.16–0.20), and a 20-item factorability audit is only marginal (KMO = 0.60). The indices are therefore interpreted as descriptive measures rather than validated latent scales. At the predictive level, AI literacy and algorithmic-manipulation awareness are significant positive predictors of the composite chatbot-trust/consumer-protection score, whereas consumer-rights awareness is not statistically significant at the 5% level. The disclosure-conditioned trust item shows limited evidence of association with the protection/safeguard index (B = 0.004, p = 0.858). Algorithmic-manipulation awareness has the largest positive coefficient in the protection-index model (B = 0.192, p < .001). The pattern motivates an exploratory distinction between disclosure-conditioned trust and safeguard endorsement, while low internal consistency limits broader construct-level conclusions. The study informs discussion of transparency, human escalation, business accountability and complaint mechanisms as conditions of justified reliance in AI-mediated commerce.

documents.abstract: During the 2024 US election, voters going online were inundated with news, information and analysis to guide their engagement with a core democratic function. However, these online spaces increasingly featured new contributions through AI-driven tools like ChatGPT. While promising to empower users, their presence also introduced new causes for uncertainty and suspicion. To identify their impact, this study investigated how references to AI were used to elicit trust or provoke distrust in news and political forums on Reddit during the election’s final days. 220,373 posts and comments from five major political subreddits revealed thematic patterns linking AI to broader societal anxieties over the reliability and transparency of news ecosystems. Four themes emerged: AI accusations to provoke distrust, Appreciation for AI, AI inaccuracy and incompetency, and AI as a threat. Users expressed appreciation for the tools, but accusations of undeclared use stoked distrust in AI, users and the platform itself.

documents.abstract: OCCUPATIONAL APPLICATIONThis study found that high emotional trust in Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS) showed a non-significant tendency toward slower manual intervention during malfunctions, and that an operator's personality was related to specific information needs. For practitioners, this indicates a critical safety gap where affective comfort, feeling "too safe" reduces readiness. To mitigate these risks, organizations should prioritize hands-on, simulated malfunction training. By exposing operators to controlled scenarios such as "phantom braking" events, practitioners can help them experience system limitations firsthand, rebuilding the protective skepticism and preparedness that sustained automation use tends to erode. Because occupational driving spans a range of operational models, safety protocols should be tailored accordingly. In managed fleets, organizations have an opportunity to implement personality-aligned Human-Machine Interface (HMI) configurations that address the specific cognitive and informational needs of individual drivers. For "Bring Your Own Device" (BYOD) gig platforms, where organizations cannot modify the vehicle's native systems, broader software-based interventions are more practical, for example, in-app geofenced warnings that alert drivers as they approach known ADAS limitation zones. Together, these targeted, context-sensitive interventions help recalibrate trust and prevent overreliance, supporting rapid recovery and sustained situational awareness across the diverse occupational contexts in which ADAS is now used.

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI)-powered versatile robotics can support agile manufacturing through adaptive task execution, multi-tasking, reconfiguration and continuous skill acquisition. However, successful deployment in industrial environments depends not only on technical performance, but also on workforce acceptance, trustworthy AI governance, interoperability with existing systems and compliance with evolving European requirements for safe and human-centric AI. This paper presents an interdisciplinary sociotechnical analysis of AI-powered versatile robotics for agile production, developed in the context of the Horizon Europe AGIMUS project. Methods A mixed-methods research design combined desk research, semi-structured interviews with 22 technical, industrial and ethics experts, industrial pilot case studies, and an online survey of 180 respondents from 16 European countries. The survey was conducted in March 2023. Given the rapid evolution of AI regulation, industrial robotics and generative AI-enabled human-robot interaction since then, the survey results are interpreted as a time-specific baseline rather than a real-time measurement of current market attitudes. Results The findings show that reliability, maintainability, increased accuracy, and adaptability were the most critical technical needs for industrial uptake, while technical robustness and safety, privacy and data governance, and transparency were comparatively difficult to achieve. Potential workforce resistance was associated primarily with job-security and role-identity concerns: fear of job loss, changes in work routines and perceived devaluation of human labour were stronger opposition factors than physical safety concerns. Acceptance measures receiving the strongest support included clear communication of operational changes, educational and training programmes, workforce-retention plans, and comprehensive briefing on the scope of robotics implementation. Conclusions The paper contributes a baseline framework for design, piloting and governance of trustworthy, human-centric, and industrially feasible robotic systems. Its practical value lies in combining technical requirements with ethical, organisational, and temporal interpretation criteria, supporting AGIMUS development and longitudinal assessment of AI-powered robotics adoption.

documents.abstract: Public organizations can delegate cognitive work to artificial intelligence while losing the capacity to scrutinize or resume that work. When does useful delegation become institutional dependence? This article develops a theory of institutional AI dependence as a task–role–workflow configuration combining substantial delegation of core cognition with insufficient task-required review or recovery capacity. It distinguishes two vulnerabilities: inadequate challenge during AI-supported work and inadequate capacity to continue judgment-intensive work when the system is unavailable. Extensive delegation with adequate distributed expertise and tested recovery constitutes managed delegation. Integrating cognitive offloading, automation, organizational learning, and public-administration research, the article extends Song et al.’s (2026) account of epistemic authority to organizational workflows and distinguishes perceived credibility from procedural authority embedded in defaults and override rules. Seven propositions connect practice displacement, challenge behavior, knowledge retention, subsequent delegation, and responsibility–control alignment. They specify how task-relevant practice, diagnostic feedback, and transferable knowledge shape retained capacity over time. The contribution is a task-relative diagnosis of threatened administrative judgment and a set of testable formation mechanisms. The framework guides public organizations in governing current agentic systems and preparing review and recovery arrangements for more capable AI.

documents.abstract: Can humans and artificial intelligence cooperate such that their combination yields greater accuracy than either agent alone? This result, termed \emph{synergy} or \emph{complementarity}, is notoriously difficult to achieve, even when both agents possess significant independent accuracy. In this paper, we present a formal framework to model human-AI interaction through the lens of reliance patterns, which characterize the joint correctness structure of human and algorithmic decisions. We derive mathematically necessary and sufficient conditions for synergy, demonstrating that its emergence depends on the ability of either agent to identify and correct the errors of the other, what we call Human and Algorithmic Correction. Beyond its theoretical contribution, the proposed framework provides a foundation for the design and evaluation of knowledge-based decision support systems, where interaction policies must dynamically integrate heterogeneous sources of expertise. We demonstrate this through the analysis of seven clinical case studies. Our empirical results reveal a ``dominance trap,'' where a strong algorithmic advantage can paradoxically inhibit synergy by eroding human corrective intervention. We also show that synergy can persist even in the presence of cognitive biases, such as automation bias, provided there is functional de-correlation between human and AI errors. These results provide a formal foundation for key concepts in the human-AI systems literature and offer actionable insights for designing interaction-centric AI systems that foster complementarity.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can make health explanations accessible while separating persuasive language from inspectable evidence. This creates a public health problem beyond plainly false content: an answer may mislead through unsupported attribution, obsolete evidence, omitted uncertainty, or inappropriate application. This Conceptual Analysis uses a targeted integrative approach to connect health literacy, misinformation, trust, large language model evaluation, and content provenance around the pathway from a generated claim to a health decision. Its contribution is an integration and operationalization of established concepts, not a new literacy construct or truth-certification mechanism. We distinguish five source traceability functions: origin, claim, evidentiary, procedural, and correction traceability. These functions interact with four iterative, context-dependent user practices: inspect, triangulate, calibrate, and escalate. Calibrated trust means discriminating between stronger and weaker support and relying proportionately on it, rather than maximizing or minimizing trust. Effective traceability also requires accessible, comprehensible evidence pathways and reasonable verification effort. Institutional and platform accountability is therefore part of the model, not an optional supplement to individual competence. We provide illustrative operational indicators, provisional risk-tiered safeguards, and six testable propositions organized around evidentiary discrimination, confidence calibration, decision appropriateness, verification behavior, verification burden, and escalation behavior. Neither the unified model nor its indicators or risk tiers have been empirically validated. The framework offers a decision-oriented research and design architecture for evaluating when evidence visibility and literacy can jointly support safer use of synthetic health information.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can influence user trust and decision-making through subtle linguistic cues, yet the behavioral effects of manipulative outputs remain poorly quantified. We introduce a behavioral computing framework for measuring \textit{behavioral vulnerability}, defined as users' susceptibility to manipulative AI responses. Building on DarkPatterns-LLM benchmark, we generate controlled manipulative stimuli using Manipulation Gradient Descent (MGD), targeting biases associated with authority, urgency, and social proof. We analyze participant responses using the Multi-Stakeholder Impact Assessment Network (MSIAN) to model cross-user influence and the Temporal Harm Propagation Model (THPM) to characterize the persistence of behavioral effects over time. In a study involving 120 participants, manipulative framing produced significant changes in trust calibration and compliance ($p < 0.01$), with effects also propagating across social contexts. These findings highlight the need to extend LLM safety evaluation beyond model outputs to measurable behavioral consequences and provide a computational framework for quantifying individual, social, and temporal risks arising from manipulative AI interactions.

documents.abstract: Abstract Research Summary To promote entrepreneurship and new business development, firms will increasingly rely on new forms of knowledge creation to manage environments marked by technological change and radical uncertainty. We argue that as generative artificial intelligence (Gen‐AI) becomes embedded in organizational processes, knowledge creation will no longer remain solely a human activity. Instead, it will increasingly emerge from hybrid interactions between human actors and firm‐specific, closed Gen‐AI systems. These systems begin to participate directly in how knowledge is generated, recombined, internalized, shared, and converted into entrepreneurial initiatives such as corporate entrepreneurship, spin‐offs, and new business models. We also reconceptualize organizational knowledge creation as a hybrid human–AI process and propose a reordered knowledge creation cycle that induces multiple knowledge spirals, captures the emergence of new agents, and the generation of diverse types of knowledge, with faster temporal dynamics. Building on this perspective, we offer a research agenda for future scholarship. Managerial Summary We discuss how firm‐specific generative AI systems are likely to fundamentally alter the ways firms generate knowledge, respond to change, and sustain long‐term renewal. We propose that rather than replacing human judgment, closed Gen‐AI changes where knowledge originates as well as how quickly it evolves, and how broadly it circulates across organizational boundaries. This means that the managerial challenge is less about adopting AI and more about designing knowledge systems and structuring knowledge flows. Executives and entrepreneurs alike need to decide how to structure human–AI collaborations, how much autonomy to grant closed Gen‐AI systems, and how to prevent speed from overwhelming sensemaking. Our work underscores that although hybrid knowledge creation promises faster and more diverse learning, it also introduces risks related to opacity, trust, and cognitive lock‐in. Firms that deliberately orchestrate the role of closed Gen‐AI in their learning systems will be better positioned to shape future advantage by promoting innovation and entrepreneurial activities of different types.

Robot-hosted quiz games depend on the robot deciding correctly which player buzzed first. Studies of robot games rarely ask how errors in such decisions affect players. We propose the Algorithmic Precision–Motivation Relationship (APMR), a model in which the precision (correctness and timeliness) of a robot's perception shapes interaction coherence, players' appraisals of competence and trust, engagement and, ultimately, motivation. We test its central prediction in a buzzer quiz hosted by a Pepper robot. Two first-responder detectors were compared: a convolutional recurrent neural network with attention (CRNN) and a training-free frequency-domain cross-correlation (CC) method that matches Mel-spectrograms against class templates recorded in the room. Offline, the CRNN was more accurate on matched laboratory data. Under synthetic-to-real transfer, however, its accuracy fell to 0.66, against 0.91 for CC, and CC was about ten times faster (23.4 vs. 226.6 ms). Forty university students, randomly assigned to teams and conditions, then played the same quiz in a between-subjects study, 20 per detector. In live play, CC named the correct first responder in 87% of buzzer events and responded in 28 ms, against 69% and 300 ms for the CRNN. On the Intrinsic Motivation Inventory, players in the CC condition reported higher Interest/Enjoyment (d = 1.62), Effort/Importance (d = 1.90) and Perceived Competence (d = 1.07), and lower Pressure/Tension (d = 0.80). Perceived Choice did not differ (d = 0.21). The results are consistent with APMR's central prediction, although accuracy and speed differed together. Designers of robot-hosted games should treat perception reliability as a game design variable, not only as an engineering metric.

Large language models (LLMs) now answer product questions, recommend items and help close deals in online shops, banks and telecom services. Customers react to these AI sales agents in two opposite ways. Some avoid them, a pattern researchers call algorithm aversion, while others prefer them to human advice, a pattern called algorithm appreciation. This paper reviews the main empirical studies on both patterns and asks how each one forms when the "algorithm" is a conversational sales agent. Drawing on research in judgment and decision making, consumer behavior and human computer interaction, it proposes a framework with three layers. The first layer contains the cues that an LLM sales agent gives off. The second layer contains five psychological pathways that operate during the conversation: competence belief, error sensitivity, empathy and uniqueness concern, social presence, and perceived control. The third layer contains situational conditions such as product type, the timing of AI identity disclosure, the customer's emotional state and prior AI experience. Six propositions are derived. The paper argues that aversion and appreciation are not fixed traits of customers but outcomes of how these layers combine in a particular sales encounter, and it discusses implications for firms and for future student research.

Slides of a lecture given at the AIOS multiplier event (Bologna, 20 October 2026, online), addressed mainly to Computer Science students preparing a thesis. The lecture discusses how generative AI changes each stage of a thesis, from literature search to writing, and how Open Science practices make the resulting work inspectable, reproducible and reusable. A hypothetical running example, a thesis on LLM-assisted unit test generation, illustrates research questions and related work, research design and decision logs, effectiveness metrics (mutation score, coverage, defect detection, effort), FAIR principles, Software Heritage and reproducibility packages. The lecture also covers the independent verification of AI output and the competences a thesis requires (DigComp, ResearchComp, ESCO). It ends with a checklist for students. The final part is self-critical: it examines how the lecture itself was prepared and where it failed to follow its own Open Science advice. It closes with an Open Science statement for the lecture.

Introduction: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has increased its presence in qualitative research studies. These tools bring opportunities and risks that need to be considered because of the type of information involved in studies with human participants. Objective: To present a proposal that contributes to the discussion of the tasks in which AI may intervene without putting methodological and ethical principles at risk. Method: Critical and focused review of literature published between 2023 and 2026, a period in which the use of language models expanded in qualitative research. The material was organized according to the use of models, the type of information, the human decisions made during the process, and ethical considerations. Results: The analysis made it possible to define four dimensions for making decisions about the use of technology: methodological coherence, proximity to the interpretive core, exposure of information, and the verifiability of technological involvement. These dimensions were used to create a three-level traffic-light system for the use of these technologies. Conclusions: The use of AI does not depend only on the model being used. Human participation and responsibility are needed to ensure methodological coherence, protect confidential information, and verify and trace findings against the original corpus. The researcher is responsible for every decision made throughout the entire process.

documents.abstract: This study aimed to evaluate undergraduate medical students’ awareness, use, perceived competence, and educational expectations regarding artificial intelligence (AI), three-dimensional portable document format (3D PDF), and deep learning in anatomy education. Data from 607 valid questionnaire responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics and chi-square tests of independence. Awareness of AI tools was high, with ChatGPT being the most recognized platform, followed by Gemini and OpenAI. Students mainly used AI to acquire theoretical knowledge, and AI use during studying anatomy ( p = 0.012). The frequency of AI use also varied according to both gender ( p = 0.028) and grade ( p = 0.010). Students reported a need for support in technical use, reliability checks, and ethical principles. Self-rated AI competence was generally moderate and differed significantly by gender ( p < 0.001). Deep learning was less familiar than AI and 3D PDFs. The use of 3D PDFs differed significantly by gender ( p = 0.025) and grade ( p = 0.028). Students considered 3D PDFs most applicable to anatomy education, followed by medical imaging and surgical planning ( p < 0.001). Overall, the findings indicate high digital awareness among medical students but limited structured preparation for responsible AI use, deep learning literacy, and visualization-based anatomical learning. Artificial intelligence is frequently described as if increasing computational capability were equivalent to increasing intelligence. This article rejects that scalar assumption and repositions artificial systems within a broader account of Natural Human Learning. It synthesises the 2026 Benjamin et al. work on cCC*, agency, bounded choice, Socialwork*, AEIOUF and consciousing; the Benjamin-McLaughlin account of Applied Curiosity and Augmented Understanding; the Benjamin-Palmer development of W-ALL as an externalised, revisable learning field; and the Natural Learning triptych's account of embodied, pre-verbal and AI-age learning. The synthesis is named LUMO: a human-governed learning environment in which machine generation enlarges the field of chances without displacing human authorship of choices, changes, responsibility or meaning. The paper advances four connected claims. First, learning begins before artificial representation - and before language: natural processes, embodiment, neural dynamics, encounter and difference provide the "horse" before the computational "cart". Second, uniquely human active agency (AAA) is categorical rather than scalar: capability may increase, but agency is not made "super" by more computation. Third, cCC* (Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes) is operationalised through the sequential AEIOUF process, A → E → I → O → U → F, with Conative Situational Integration (CSI) maintaining continuity across transitions. Fourth, LUMO should be coupled to protected canonical infrastructure: LUMO supports porous exploration; LIMO, with PROTON guardrails, protects provenance, permissions, canonical state and authorised change. R1-R16 and the 96-facet R × AEIOUF address space provide a selective-context routing layer, while CQI and CGI distinguish inquiry from generative construction. In the age of AI, the binding criterion becomes the preservation of the learner's CAN before externally supplied COULD. The resulting architecture reframes AI as a contingent support to human Natural Learning rather than its model, endpoint or successor. Sixteen research propositions are specified for empirical evaluation.

Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a transformative technology in higher education, significantly influencing the way students learn, access information, complete academic tasks, and develop professional skills. Tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Canva AI have become increasingly popular among commerce students for assignments, presentations, exam preparation, and concept clarification. While these technologies offer opportunities for personalized and efficient learning, their growing use also raises concerns regarding academic integrity, ethical practices, critical thinking, and dependency on AI-generated content. This study aims to examine the adoption and responsible use of Generative AI tools among commerce students in higher education and to evaluate their contribution towards sustainable learning. The research adopts a descriptive and analytical research design using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire administered to commerce students. The study focuses on students' awareness of GenAI tools, frequency and purpose of usage, responsible AI practices, AI dependency, and the perceived impact of AI on academic productivity and sustainable learning outcomes. The study is expected to provide insights into how commerce students integrate Generative AI into their academic learning and whether they use these tools responsibly by verifying information, avoiding plagiarism, and using AI as a learning aid rather than a substitute for independent thinking. It also explores the relationship between AI adoption, ethical usage, and sustainable learning practices in the context of higher education. The findings of this research are expected to assist educators, higher education institutions, and policymakers in designing AI literacy initiatives, promoting responsible AI usage, and developing pedagogical practices aligned with the objectives of sustainable and inclusive education. The study contributes to the growing body of literature on Artificial Intelligence in commerce education by emphasizing the importance of balancing technological innovation with ethical responsibility and lifelong learning in higher education. Keywords: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), Responsible AI, Sustainable Learning, Commerce Students, Higher Education, AI Ethics, Academic Productivity, Digital Literacy.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping the future of higher education, tasking educators with transforming teaching, learning, and assessment practices to consider how AI can enhance the educational environment. With its increasing availability, it is important for administrators, faculty, and students to explore the practical nature of AI use prior to entry into the workforce. Faculty must also reevaluate how they approach assessing student learning, tasking them to rethink each assessment’s purpose, how it will inform future practice, and how it will prepare learners to use AI. Furthermore, faculty must also be prepared to consider the collaborative nature of AI, transforming their mindset to consider AI as an active co-designer and partner, one that does not seek to diminish the educator’s human judgment. This manuscript will articulate the importance of co-design, where AI and educators collaboratively shape assessment tools, and serve to champion feedback partnerships that enhance reflective practice for both students and faculty.

documents.abstract: Abstract Entrepreneurship education (EE) is increasingly extending across disciplines and institutional contexts, creating pressure to sustain the facilitation, reflection and contextual responsiveness required by experiential learning. At the same time, the rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education raises questions about how AI can support such experiential learning without assuming authority over the judgement and decision-making central to entrepreneurial action. This study develops and empirically examines an AI-as-intern design logic for experiential EE. Rather than positioning AI as an authoritative “oracle”, the framework establishes an intentionally asymmetric human-AI partnership. Here AI provides prompts, alternatives, provisional representations and process support, while learners and educators retain responsibility for contextual interpretation, evaluative judgement and consequential decisions. The study examines two postgraduate entrepreneurship cohorts at a UK university ( n = 60) using a custom AI-enabled platform integrated into normal teaching. Evidence comprised session recordings and transcripts, observational field notes, a post-workshop survey, and 12 semi-structured interviews. Findings show that students used AI primarily as process scaffolding and iterative support. Learners accepted, rejected, modified and combined AI-generated material, while team interaction created additional opportunities for scrutiny and contextual evaluation. Our findings do not establish improvements in students’ judgement, creativity or cognitive load, but do show how these activities remained active within a bounded human-AI arrangement. The paper contributes a pedagogic design logic for AI-enabled experiential EE and provides exploratory propositions for the design of human-AI pedagogy concerning human authority, evaluative judgement, collaborative oversight, creative sequencing and bounded scaffolding under conditions of scaling pressure.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can convert movement into scores, visual overlays, and corrective prompts, but technical precision does not determine how learners interpret that feedback. We develop a motivational-meaning model for university physical education (PE), integrating self-determination theory, feedback literacy, self-regulated learning, and motor-learning research. Its contribution is a context-specific account of how pedagogical framing, social visibility, and embodied verification organize the interpretation of an AI-feedback event. Informational and controlling meaning are distinguished from subsequent psychological-need experiences. Blocked translation denotes a temporary difficulty establishing a defensible basis for action, rather than a third motivational meaning. The model also proposes self-regulatory appropriation as the transfer of an externally supported feedback process into independent monitoring and adjustment; its distinctiveness from established self-regulation constructs remains an empirical question. Seven proposition groups specify separable predictions concerning framing, actionable information, contestability, evaluative exposure, discrepancy repair, skill transfer, and a secondary pathway to continued participation. The outcome structure distinguishes system engagement, acquisition performance, retention and transfer, affect and well-being, and voluntary physical activity. Continued participation is treated as a distal hypothesis requiring longitudinal evidence and attention to prior activity, health, habit, and opportunity. We outline independent measurement of event interpretation and need experience, tests that separate technical from perceived accuracy, and ethical, multilevel research designs. The model offers testable design principles rather than evidence that AI feedback improves learning or participation.

The global smart cockpit market is undergoing explosive growth, with AI-enabled functionalities emerging as core components of modern vehicles. However, the integration of AI in smart cockpits has introduced complex compliance challenges under the EU AI Act and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). This paper adopts a three-dimensional analytical framework (regulatory, technical, industrial practice) to systematically explore the compliance landscape, key dilemmas, and actionable solutions for smart cockpit AI systems. First, the paper clarifies the core obligations of high-risk and limited-risk AI systems under the EU regulatory framework. It also analyzes cross-regional regulatory conflicts among the EU, China, and the U.S., highlighting differences in data localization, consent mechanisms, and conformity assessment requirements. Second, the paper identifies risk-tier-specific compliance challenges, including data bias, transparency deficits, cross-border data transfer risks, as well as lifecycle management burdens. Additionally, it addresses emerging challenges brought by the integration of large language models (LLMs) in in-vehicle ecosystems, such as training data copyright verification and generative content controllability. Finally, the paper proposes an integrated compliance strategy. This strategy encompasses technical paths, full-lifecycle management, and cross-regional modular design to adapt to divergent regulatory requirements. The research provides a standardized compliance framework and practical tools for global automakers, helping balance technical innovation, user experience, and regulatory compliance to drive the sustainable development of the intelligent automotive industry.

documents.abstract: Abstract In today’s technology-driven world, Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of higher education. College students are increasingly using AI tools such as ChatGPT, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, Claude, and Perplexity AI for their academic work. These tools help students prepare assignments and presentations, understand difficult topics, find ideas, improve their writing, and complete academic tasks in less time. However, simply knowing how to use AI is not enough. Students also need to understand whether the information provided by AI is correct, how to use it responsibly, and what problems may arise from depending too much on these tools. This study focuses on understanding the level of AI literacy among college students and its relationship with their academic performance. It will also study how familiar students are with generative AI tools, how often they use them, and for what academic purposes. The study will further examine the benefits students experience, the difficulties they face, and their understanding of issues such as academic honesty, originality, privacy, and responsible use of AI. The study will use a mixed-methods research design, combining both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative information will be collected through a structured questionnaire using Google Forms. Interviews and open-ended questions will be used to understand students’ personal experiences, opinions, and attitudes towards AI in education. The study will include college students between 18 and 26 years of age from different academic backgrounds. The research will be limited to colleges in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. The study is expected to provide a clear picture of how AI literacy is connected with students’ academic performance. The findings may also help colleges and teachers plan AI literacy programmes and create practical guidelines for the proper use of AI in education. Overall, the study aims to encourage students to use AI as a helpful learning tool while maintaining independent thinking, originality, and academic responsibility.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now helps people write essays, reports, and even personal speeches, but people who use it can pay a social price through negative interpersonal judgement. We investigated whether people judge AI users as less moral, potential boundary conditions, and whether the policies that institutions set about AI use change this judgement. In six preregistered experiments with 2,183 participants from Belgium, the United States, and the United Kingdom, participants evaluated people who completed tasks either with or without AI assistance. AI users were consistently rated as less moral, as having invested less effort, as less deserving of their result, and as less attractive collaboration partners. The penalty was large, generalizable across context, and did not require a direct comparison with a non-user. Across studies, people who perceived a larger effort gap also judged the AI user more harshly. When the use of AI had been explicitly permitted, the moral penalty was attenuated by more than a third and when AI use had been prohibited, the penalty further increased. Clear AI policies may therefore reduce, but not remove, the reputational costs of using AI.
